title: Torch & Crypt dungeon crawler
author: NullPacketLost
selftext:
**About me:** I'm not a software developer but like to tinker on my free time.

Yes, this text is also written with the help of AI.

**What this is:** I’ve been building Torch & Crypt, a free-to-play isometric roguelike that runs directly in the browser (no install, no account, no monetization): [https://dungeon.bytemind.dev](https://dungeon.bytemind.dev)

Instead of using Unity/Godot or external sprite packs, the whole thing runs on a custom TypeScript software pixel renderer (HTML5 Canvas), procedural voxel sprites, dynamic torch lighting + fog of war, procedural WebAudio SFX, and a FastAPI + SQLite backend with HMAC-verified leaderboards and Hardcore mode.

**How AI was used in the workflow.**

Tools used: Gemini Antigravity Orchestrator (Neon) and Suno.

Plan-first & surgical edits: Early on, letting the AI rewrite large files caused regressions fast. What actually made a 100+ iteration codebase maintainable was adding strict project rules: forcing a short plan before touching code, keeping edits surgical, and never letting it touch unrelated systems.

Automated verification loop: Every change goes through tsc --noEmit, a 58-test TypeScript engine test suite (covering dungeon generation, LOS occlusion, pathfinding, loot rolls, and save snapshots), and Python API tests before deploying to Docker.

Human-in-the-loop game feel: AI was great for scaffolding systems, refactoring modules, and building a LAN-only Admin Portal to tune monster stats, drop rates, and audio live. But I still had to playtest heavily to catch subtle feel bugs. For example, monsters getting stuck vibrating around pillars, cutting corners through lava pools, or aggroing through thin wall corners all showed up in real playtests, and we turned each one into permanent regression tests alongside a flow-field + bounded pathfinder.

Hosting: Self-hosted in Docker container behind Nginx and a Cloudflare Tunnel.

**What worked / what didn't.**

Worked well: Modularizing the engine early (separate rendering, AI, pathfinding, combat, loot, and UI layers) and writing deterministic unit tests for every bug fix so the AI couldn't silently re-break old mechanics.

Struggled: Visual polish, lighting/contrast tuning, and combat pacing. Telling an LLM "make combat feel snappier" rarely works on the first shot—short gameplay clips, screenshots, and specific numeric constraints worked much better.

Happy to share more details on workflow if anyone’s curious.  
But it's mostly /plan \[idea\] and proceed or scrap.

About the code? Not so much as I haven't even looked at it. 😓 

Will I continue with this specific project? I would say maybe.
